standouts.title: $5T opportunity: AI Roll Ups
standouts.summary: Greg Isenberg's solo breakdown of the silver-tsunami thesis: ~1 million small businesses worth roughly $5T are expected to change hands by 2035 as their owners retire, and AI agents now do the work those firms run on. Thrive Holdings and General Catalyst are already running the fund playbook, and he argues the small-deal gap is wide open for solo founders.
args: The fund playbook is proven at scale: build the AI/agent platform first, buy a trusted firm, run agents in the background. Thrive has bought ~50 accounting firms (at Larson Gross, Codex-built AI processed 7,000 returns this tax season while accountants saved 31% of their time); General Catalyst put $1.5B behind Long Lake/Crescendo (18 property management acquisitions, ~$100M EBITDA). Margins move from 5-10% toward 30-40% if the thesis holds.

Big funds skip the small deals, which is the opening: a billion-dollar fund won't touch a $2M bookkeeping firm, and many retiring owners would rather hand their life's work to a person than a fund. The one-person holdco runs a shared agent platform across businesses, puts a GM with real upside at each, and keeps a human approval rule on all agent output.
The most valuable asset in the holdco is boring: the corrections log, turned into rules every week, compounding into institutional knowledge no fund can replicate.

The bear case, steelmanned: the headline numbers come from young VC-backed operators that haven't faced a recession, so read them as direction, not proof. And the playbook only works if agents get quietly integrated without breaking client trust.
standouts.why: This is the most directly relevant episode in weeks. Accounting firms are the rollup target, and you're a CA who speaks both accounting-firm operations and AI agents. Two plays worth considering: (a) advise rollup funds or retiring owners as the data/AI-readiness layer, or (b) build the shared agent platform small accounting firms would need. Content idea: a LinkedIn post on what the $5T retirement wave meeting AI agents means for mid-size accounting firms. Question to explore, not advice: would you ever want to run one of these firms yourself, or stay on the platform/advisory side?

standouts.show: All-In with Chamath, Jason, Sacks & Friedberg
standouts.title: Daniel Ek: Life After Spotify, Broken Healthcare Incentives, Catching Disease Early & AI's Potential
standouts.summary: Ek's first long sit-down since stepping back from Spotify: how he beat piracy by betting his own money on the labels, then applied the Spotify playbook to healthcare through Neko Health's $499 full-body scan, and closed on AI, open vs. closed models, and regulating compute.
args: The Spotify playbook, aimed at health: accumulate more data than incumbents, then predict. Neko's annual visit draws 53 blood markers, captures 6,000 high-res skin images, and gives you an hour with a clinician and results on the spot, for $499.

The structural trap in US healthcare: the system spends ~18% of GDP treating people after they get sick, because employment-tied insurance means no payer can capture the 10-to-20-year return on prevention. Ek's fix is to shrink the bet so small, with positive unit economics, that someone funds it anyway.

On AI: tech has failed to sell the upside of AI to the public; the panel and Ek work through open vs. closed models and whether compute gets regulated. Ek lands the founder's version of the same point he made on healthcare: data moats decide who wins.
standouts.why: Two angles. Health: you're the quantified-self archetype Neko is betting on (Dexcom, WHOOP, labs on demand), so watch the US clinic rollout as a buyer, not just a spectator. Business: "make the bet so small it's fundable" is a framing device for Alpha Infra proposals — cheap pilots with positive unit economics beat transformation pitches. It also connects straight to yesterday's All-In open-source thread: the open vs. closed model debate keeps showing up in your client conversations.

standouts.title: Jason's Put a $5K Bounty on His Dream Chrome Extension | E2338
standouts.summary: Jason posted a $5,000 bounty on a product idea he'd been sitting on for 20 years, asked vibecode experts to build it, and got dozens of submissions. The frame that matters: a product that would have cost $500,000 to build in 2006 now costs less than a used car.
args: Build costs collapsed by an order of magnitude or more. What's demo-able today by one person with AI tooling used to take a funded team.
Bounties are a procurement mechanism, not a gimmick: $5K in prize money attracted dozens of working submissions, faster and cheaper than scoping a dev shop.
The judging is the real work: reviewing the top 3 submissions teaches you how to spec, which is the skill clients now need most.
standouts.why: This is a sellable Alpha Infra move. Offer clients the "bounty a prototype" play: fixed-fee, days-not-months working prototypes before anyone commits to a build. It de-risks the buy decision and makes you the person who taught them to spec. Content idea: ask your network what 20-year-old product idea they'd bounty today.

standouts.title: Baird out, Saffas win and Japanese wides
standouts.summary: TGC's two-hour world tour: Firdose Moonda previews South Africa's upcoming summer, Peter Lalor breaks down Mike Baird's exit from Cricket Australia, Dan Cherny covers Australia A and the SA series, Ali Martin wraps England's summer, and Japan's Declan Suzuki explains the wide call that blew up the Japan-India game.
args: Baird is out: CA chair Mike Baird stepped down Sep 28 after Cricket NSW withdrew support over the Big Bash privatisation push (starting with the Melbourne Renegades sale). David Boon takes over as interim chair on Oct 28.

The privatisation still moves: CA is selling the Renegades licence while keeping control of international scheduling, player availability, salary caps and media rights. Licences get privatised, the competition stays governed — the IPL-era capital structure is arriving in Australia.
The governance lesson: Baird lost his own state's backing and couldn't push an equity deal through without it. Stakeholder vetoes decide board deals, not the numbers.
standouts.why: SA expat first — the summer preview with Firdose is your lane, good background listening this week. Sports-business angle from your MLC days: the licence-sale model is worth understanding as it spreads. And the Baird story is a clean case study on stakeholder politics killing a deal — same dynamic that kills consulting engagements and partnerships.
